scoreNote: Strong (5): grants the large role of chance in discovery while showing that accident becomes discovery only through a prepared, persistent mind; concrete examples and a clear synthesis.

sentences.text: The story of science is full of happy accidents: penicillin from a contaminated dish, X-rays from a stray glow, the microwave from a melted chocolate bar.
The statement generalizes from such tales, claiming that many important discoveries are accidental, stumbled upon while seeking the answer to some other question.

The statement is partly true, because chance genuinely plays a large role in discovery, but it tells only half the story, since accidents become discoveries only in the hands of a prepared and persistent mind.

sections.role: Body — Accident really does drive discovery

sentences.text: It is true that accident has shaped an astonishing number of important findings.
Fleming was not hunting for antibiotics when a stray mould killed his bacteria, and Roentgen was not looking for X-rays when an unexpected glow lit his laboratory.
Research is a journey into the unknown, and the unknown, by definition, holds surprises that no plan can anticipate.
Often the question a scientist sets out to answer turns out to be less important than the strange result he happens to notice along the way.
Whole fields have opened because someone was studying one thing and tripped over another.
The history of medicine, chemistry, and physics is studded with breakthroughs that arrived sideways, while their discoverers were looking elsewhere.
So the statement captures something real: discovery is far less orderly than the textbooks suggest.

sections.role: Body — But accident is not enough

sentences.text: However, to call these discoveries simply accidental is to overlook the crucial half of the story.
The same mould had landed on countless dishes before Fleming, and the same glow had surely been seen by others, yet they noticed nothing of importance.
An accident becomes a discovery only when a trained, alert mind recognizes that something unexpected and significant has occurred.
As Pasteur observed, chance favors the prepared mind, and the preparation is doing every bit as much work as the chance.
It took years of expertise for Fleming to grasp what his ruined experiment meant, and more years of others' labor to turn the observation into a medicine.
A thousand people spill their coffee; only the one already thinking hard about a problem sees in the spill the answer to it.
Recognizing an anomaly as important, rather than dismissing it as a flaw, is itself a hard-won skill.
The lucky observation is simply wasted on a mind that does not know what it is looking at.
The accident supplies the opportunity, but knowledge, attention, and persistence supply the discovery.
Moreover, the fuller truth is that discovery is born of chance and preparation working together.
Neither alone suffices: planning without surprise rarely yields anything new, but surprise without a prepared observer yields nothing at all.
This is why important accidents cluster among those who work hardest and know most, not among the idle or the ignorant.
Serendipity is not the opposite of effort but its frequent reward.
In conclusion, the statement is right that accident matters greatly but wrong to leave the matter there.
Important discoveries are indeed often stumbled upon, but the stumbling becomes a discovery only because a knowledgeable, watchful mind is present to recognize it.
Chance may open the door, but it takes a prepared mind to walk through it.
